newsitem.title: SPAIN: Reuter poll sees Spain borderline on euro criteria.
newsitem.headline: Reuter poll sees Spain borderline on euro criteria.

text.p: In the crucial 1997 tests of inflation and deficit for Europe's single currency, Spain will be teetering on the borderline, a new Reuters poll showed.
Its numbers will be neither good enough to guarantee entry nor bad enough to ensure rejection, analysts predicted.
Spain, like the rest of the euro pretenders, will be put to the test in 1997 on five economic criteria which determine fitness for the planned launch in 1999.
On several key points, Spain will be hovering on the edge of acceptability, the survey of 10 economists from international banks showed.

The minority Popular Party government, which took over this spring after 13 years of Socialist rule, has put the single currency at the top of its agenda and has pushed through a tight budget to ensure Spain is ready.

While the government is not expected to face problems on long-term interest rates, currency stability or debt -- which, as in many countries, is above permissable limits but is declining -- analysts see it closing in on the deficit and inflation targets.
"From an economic point of view we could be in. I think we're on the right side of the line," said Alfredo Urrutia, chief economist at Societe Generale in Madrid.
According to the poll conducted this week, Spain's public sector deficit in 1997 will exceed the reference value of three percent of gross domestic product, but will be trending lower.
On average, those polled expect the public sector deficit according to Maastricht criteria to be 3.32 percent in 1997, a hair above the three percent government forecast.
They see it narrowing from 4.6 percent this year, slightly above the government's expectation of 4.4 percent.
Spain does not regularly provide data on the public sector deficit according to the Maastricht Treaty, which sets out the criteria for participation in the single currency.
For inflation, analysts forecast on average a 2.77 percent rate for 1997, slower than an average 3.58 percent rise this year.

To qualify, Spain's inflation may not exceed the average of the three lowest EU member inflation rates plus 1.5 percentage points. Many economists here have said Spain will have difficulty meeting this goal as well.
The government does not forecast averages but projects December inflation at 3.4 percent over the year-earlier month, above analysts' 3.3 percent forecast.
"On CPI, I suspect the threshhold there is going to be around three percent," said Ros Lifton, chief international economist at HSBC in London.
Because the economics are close but not completely convincing, political considerations are expected to dominate the decision on who will found a single currency.
"Treaties generally embody the spirit of a plan," said Craig Schute, fixed-income economist at Bear Stearns in London.
"The fact Spain didn't meet the criteria wouldn't preclude its participation" because it has made progress toward convergence, Schute said.
